title: If they didn't laugh
hookLine: when the foolish hear of the Tao they laugh, and without their laughter it wouldn't be the Tao (Tao Te Ching 41)

cards: Someone at work sees you sit with your eyes closed for a minute at your desk and asks, half joking, whether you've fallen asleep.
Or a cousin at a family dinner raises an eyebrow at the morning walk, the candle, the phone left in another room. A small laugh. Not cruel, just puzzled.
Chapter forty-one of the Tao Te Ching saw that laugh coming, and it treats the laugh as something other than a problem.

teach.b: First, three hearers. The chapter opens with three kinds of people hearing about the way. The first hears and puts it into practice with everything they have.
The second seems to keep it one day and lose it the next. The third laughs out loud. Second, the twist.
In James Legge's translation the chapter says of that laugh: "If it were not (thus) laughed at, it would not be fit to be the Tao." The laugh is treated almost as a sign.
If the way made perfect sense to everyone at first glance, it wouldn't be the way. Third, why it looks funny.
The chapter goes straight on to things that look like their opposites: the bright way seems dim, the way forward seems to go back, the level way seems rough.
Seen from outside, slowing down looks like falling behind, and sitting still looks like doing nothing. And the chapter doesn't tell anyone to argue with the laughers, or to look down on them.
The laugh comes with the territory.

Fourth, the middle hearer. Keeping a practice for a week, then dropping it the first time somebody smirks: that's the middle hearer's pattern. Chapter forty-one offers that hearer something steadying.
The laugh doesn't prove you're wrong. It may only prove that what you're doing looks, from outside, like nothing.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often quote chapter forty-one when a practice like stillness or simplicity draws puzzled looks, taking the laugh as part of the path rather than a reason to quit.

games.q: what does “if they didn't laugh” mean?
o: proof that the mockers will someday believe too
if nobody laughed at the way, it wouldn't be the way
a reason to hide your practice from other people

s: chapter forty-one tells readers to argue with those who laugh
it just says the laugh comes with the territory.
the chapter says the way forward can seem to go back
it lists things that look like their opposites.
in the chapter, only one kind of person hears of the way
there are three hearers: one practices, one wavers, one laughs.

games.q: you've kept a quiet morning minute for a week. a friend laughs and calls it weird. what does chapter forty-one suggest?
o: drop it, since it looks odd.
keep it, and let the laugh be.
games.why: the chapter says that if the way weren't laughed at, it wouldn't be the way. it doesn't ask you to win the argument.

practice: Settle where you are, and if anyone near you could see, let them see. Let a little self-consciousness rise, the feeling of being watched doing something that looks like nothing, and keep sitting through it without pushing it away.
If you pray, this can be a quiet prayer; if you don't, two minutes of breathing on purpose.

wordCard.voice: If they didn't laugh. Chapter forty-one: when some people hear of the way, they laugh, and if they didn't, it wouldn't be the way. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: to laugh; in chapter forty-one, what the third hearer does on hearing of the Tao.

carryVoice: Your line: they laugh. A puzzled smile is no verdict on a quiet minute. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: If it were not (thus) laughed at, it would not be fit to be the Tao.
